title: Winter Games
build: Epyx original, PAL, two disk sides (C64 Preservation Project, verified dump)

records.c: Hot Dog Aerials starts here: interrupts off, the stack reset, $083D set to say the menu was loaded over, the BASIC ROM banked out ($01 = $26), the video chip in bitmap mode with multicolour on and bank 2 ($8000-$BFFF) selected through CIA 2, the CIAs' interrupts and timers off, port A of CIA 1 set to input, black border and background, and the raster interrupt at line 250 with the KERNAL's IRQ vector ($0314) at hd_irq.

The raster interrupt, twice a frame. At line 241 it switches to text mode with the character set at $9800 (the ROM's upper and lower case set, which the video chip sees in this bank), so the bottom row is text; the next interrupt is at line 251.

At line 251 (250 the first time): bitmap mode and multicolour again for the next frame's picture, the skier's sprite shapes (show_frame_ptrs), a step of the sound engine (sound_step) and the joystick (read_stick); the next interrupt at line 241, and the frame count at $10 for the main loop.
Acknowledges the raster interrupt, restores the registers the KERNAL's handler saved, and returns.

The joystick into $1F, its bits turned over so a set bit is a direction held (1 up, 2 down, 4 left, 8 right, $10 fire): port 2 with one joystick ($087D) or for odd-numbered players, port 1 for the others.

Sounds stopped, the event's tune started (sound 0), the first player and attempt; then the main loop, once a frame: by the state in $11, set up a run (hd_setup), run it (hd_run), or after it (hd_after).
An RTS nothing reaches.
After a run. In practice ($081D negative) "PLAY AGAIN?" at column 20 with YES or NO beside it: up chooses YES, down NO, fire confirms; YES starts the run again, NO goes back to the menu.
Fire on the play-again question: YES (the Y at $83E0) sets state 0 for another run; NO falls to the exit.
State 0: the next run is set up on the next frame.

In competition: the next player ($70 counts from 1 to the number of players in $081E, $72 steps through their 32-byte records); after the last, the next attempt ($71), three in all; after the third attempt, back to the menu.
Back to the menu: the stack reset and the loader's $0900, which loads the menu and starts it where it left off.
The question and its two answers for print_bottom, each a column then the text and a zero: "PLAY AGAIN?" at column 20, "YES   " and "NO    " at column 32.
Prints a string on the bottom text row ($83C0): its first byte is the column, then the characters (ASCII, which the ROM's second set shows as capitals) to a zero.

The player's name and country (16 characters from the player's record at $0800 + $72) at the left of the bottom row, spaces to the end of the row, and the player's best score so far (its six characters of text, record offset $10) at column 32 when there is one.
Unpacks each stream in the list at ($16), two bytes an address, to a zero.

Unpacks one stream at ($14), the format of the opening ceremony's pictures: a destination address, then commands of one byte, the top two bits the kind and the low six a count (0 for 64): 0, the next byte repeated; 1, that many bytes copied; 2, that many bytes skipped; 3, that many bytes each followed by two zeros. A zero byte ends it.
The stream's end.
Steps the destination at $12-$13.
Steps the source at $14-$15.

State 0, a run set up: the screen blanked, zero page $10-$6F cleared, the picture unpacked (hd_picture_list), the sprites' colours, positions and multicolour, the skier at the top of the in-run (frame 0) with the run's starting speed and gravity, and the player's name.
In competition, "ATTEMPT" and the attempt's digit at column 20; then the picture shown, and a wait for fire.
The screen on, one frame, then fire; the word cleared, the start sound (15), and state 1.
The three packed streams of the picture, for unpack_list, and a zero to end: the bitmap ($47A7), the screen's colours ($597C) and the colour RAM's ($5BF1).
The skier's eight sprites' starting positions for $D000-$D010, X and Y for each and the high bits of X.

The sprites' colours for $D025-$D02E: blue and light grey shared by the multicolour sprites, then black for the even sprites (the outlines, in hires) and orange for the odd ones (multicolour, the skin).
Nine spaces at column 20, which clear "ATTEMPT n".
"ATTEMPT" at column 20; setup_attempt puts the digit at column 28.
State 1, a frame of the run: the skier moved (move_skier) and placed (place_sprites), then the step of the run in $36, through run_steps.
The run's six steps, by the number in $36, which counts down from 4: in_air (0), arms_up (1), take_off (2), kicker (3), in_run (4), and judged (5) after the landing.
The step routines' high bytes, read one on from run_steps.

Step 0, in the air: the moves' script stepped (step_script) until the skier's Y reaches 181, the snow. Then step 5; a good landing needs the stick centred and the arms-up frame (9): the landing script and sound 9. Anything else is a fall: the moves are forgotten ($3C = $FF, so the score is 0), sound 6, and one of four falls chosen at random, with its script, speeds and sound from fall_scripts.
A good landing: the skier slides on down the slope (downward speed $48), sound 9, the landing script at $17F5.
Fire ignored, then the moves' script stepped.
The four falls: their scripts ($17C1, $17CB, $17D9, $17E5), then their sideways speeds ($0120 for the first two, which slide on, 0 for the others).
The fall scripts' addresses' high bytes, read one on from fall_scripts.
The four falls' sideways speeds, two bytes each: $0120, $0120, 0 and 0.
Their high bytes, read one on.
The four falls' downward speeds ($48, $48, 0, 0): the first two slide on down the landing slope, the others stop.
The four falls' sounds, 11 to 14.
Step 1: after four frames of frame 2, the arms-up frame (9), sounds stopped, gravity $0A, and the moves' script started at air_script.
Step 2: after two frames, frame 2, the skier rising off the kicker.
Step 3: after two more frames the kicker throws the skier up: the sideways speed $0120 and the vertical speed turned upward.
Step 4, the first: ten frames down the in-run, then frame 1, the tuck, and gravity $0A.

Step 5, after the landing: the landing's or the fall's script runs until its last pose, of 60 frames, begins ($32 = 59); then the judges' marks (judge), the tune again, in competition a pause of ten frames and fire, and state 2.

A step of the moves' script at ($30), each frame in the air. A move's pose that is held ($32 negative) counts the frames the stick stays where it was in $40; when the stick moves, a hold of 10 to 19 frames goes on with the script, any other is awkward: one more in $39, frame $1D (the move's awkward pose) for 20 frames and sound 6.
The current frame's time, in $32, counted down; at 0 the next entry.

The next entry: $FF opens the list of moves (choose_move); a frame and a time show that frame for that long; a time with bit 7 set holds the pose while the stick is held, and its third byte is the pose shown if the hold is awkward.
The frame at which the stick first left the move's direction, in $1C.

A byte with bit 7 set goes back that many bytes while the stick is still held: the move done again, counted as a second move the same as the first ($3E) and, for a flip, another rotation in $38. When the stick has been let go, the loop is left: cleanly at frame 8 or 13 (three bytes on, past the awkward pose), awkwardly at any other (one more in $39 and sound 6, and the awkward pose shown).

The list of moves at ($30): five bytes each, a stick direction, the move's number, its sound and the address of its script, to a zero. The direction held picks the move: it goes into the list at $3D on ($3C counts them), a flip (5 or 6) counts in $38, its sound starts and its script follows. With no match, the address after the zero.
Takes the next two bytes as the script's new address.

Puts the skier's eight sprites in a block of two by two, each place two sprites over each other: X from $27-$28 (the right column 24 pixels on, with the high X bits in $D010), Y from $2D (the lower row 21 lines down).
The sprite pointers for the frame shown: shapes $3B to $3B+7, the multicolour sprite of each place the even shape and the hires one over it the odd.
The skier's position moved by its speeds, in 8.8 fixed point with a fraction: X ($26-$28) by $29-$2B, Y ($2C-$2D) by $2E-$2F, and gravity ($33-$34) added to the vertical speed.

Unpacks frame $3A into the sprite shapes not on screen, $8C00 (shapes $30-$37) or $8E00 ($38-$3F), and makes those the next shown: two buffers, so a frame never changes while it is drawn. A frame is 64 groups of eight bytes: a mask byte, then the bytes its set bits stand for, the clear ones zero.
Steps the script pointer at $30-$31.
The addresses of the skier's 58 frames, by frame number: 0 to 26 from $32A3, 27 to 57 from $1A40 in another order.
The frames' addresses' high bytes, read one on from frame_table.

The script in the air: frame 9 for six frames, then the list of moves, two stunts and a flip for each side: up-left the Daffy (move 1, sound 7), up-right the back scratch (4, sound 5), down-left the mule kick (2, sound 7), down-right the swan (3, sound 5), right the forward flip (5, sound 8), left the back flip (6, sound 8). With the stick centred it starts again.
The back flip: frames 3 to 8, then round again from frame 5 while the stick is held; frame 41 when it is let go awkwardly; back to the air script.
The forward flip: frames 10 to 13, round again while held, frame 42 if awkward, frames 14 and 5.
The Daffy: frames 15 to 17, frame 18 held (frame 40 if awkward), then 19, 20 and 9.
The back scratch: frames 15 and 21 to 23, frame 26 held (45 if awkward), then 25 and 9.
The swan: frames 15, 33 and 37, frame 38 held (43 if awkward), then 39 and 9.
The mule kick: frames 15, 33 and 34, frame 35 held (44 if awkward), then 46, 36 and 9.
The first fall: frames 27 to 30, face down in the snow, sliding on down the slope.
The second fall: frames 27 to 30 and on to 32, buried in the snow.
The third fall: frames 38 and 48 to 51, thrown out of the skis into the snow. The arms-up frame after it is never reached: the judging starts on the last pose.
The fourth fall: frames 52 to 57, onto the back; the judging starts on the last pose, so the landing's script after it is not reached from here.
The landing: frame 9 for 34, 16 and 60 frames, and an empty list of moves that keeps it there.

The judges' marks. The base mark, in tenths in $23: no move 0; one stunt 6.3, one flip 7.2; with two moves (only the first two count) two of the same stunt 8.7, two different stunts 9.6, two of the same flip 9.2, two different flips or a stunt and a flip 10.0. Then 1.4 off for each awkward move in $39.

A mark of 9.0 or more gets the crowd's cheer (sound 10). The scoreboard is put over the top of the picture (show_scoreboard), then each of the eight judges' marks in turn: the base mark plus a random -0.1 to +0.2 (none for 0 or 10.0), added into $20-$21, drawn under the judge's country, with a tick (sound 4) and a pause of 20 frames.
The total, the sum divided by eight, into $16; a total better than the player's best ($0816 in the record) replaces it and its text (score_text); then a tick and the total drawn under TOTAL.
Where in the bitmap each judge's mark is drawn, the third row of the scoreboard, four characters apart.
Writes the mark in $20 as text into the player's record, offsets $10-$15: three spaces, the units, a point and the tenths, or "10.0".
Copies the scoreboard's 1,280 bytes of bitmap (hd_scoreboard) over the top four character rows of the picture, $A000-$A4FF.
Draws the mark in $16 at the bitmap address in $14-$15, a character cell for each of the units, the point and the tenths; 100 draws "10" with no point.
Copies a digit's five bytes of bitmap from digit_glyphs into the cell at ($14).
Copies the decimal point's five bytes into the cell at ($14).
Moves ($14) to the next character cell, eight bytes on.
The digits 0 to 9 for the scoreboard, five bytes of multicolour bitmap each, light figures on a dark ground.
The decimal point's five bytes; the last two bytes after it are not read.
The bytes before wait_frames decode as LDX #60, its first instruction, which no caller runs: each passes its own count.
Waits X frames.
Waits X frames, then until fire is pressed.
Waits for the interrupt's frame count at $10, then steps the random number.
The random number at $1A3D-$1A3F, 24 bits with the high byte first, shifted right once, the bit fed in at the top the exclusive or of the low byte's bits 0 and 5.
The random number's three bytes; the event reads the low two bits of $1A3D.
The random number's middle byte.
Its low byte, whose bits 0 and 5 make the next bit.
Frame 27, the first fall's start: the skier pitching forward, skis crossed.
Frame 28, the first fall: diving into the snow.
Frame 29, the fall: sliding face down with a spray of snow.
Frame 30, the fall's end: face down in the snow.
Frame 46, the mule kick coming back: leaning forward, skis together.
Frame 33, the swan's and mule kick's start: leaning forward, arms out.
Frame 34, the mule kick: skis kicked out to the side.
Frame 35, the mule kick held: skis upright beside the body.
Frame 36, after the mule kick: arms up, skis down.
Frame 31, the second fall: buried in the snow, skis sticking out.
Frame 32, the second fall's end: only a little of the skier showing.
Frame 37, the swan: arms spread.
Frame 38, the swan held, and the third fall's first frame.
Frame 39, coming out of the swan.
Frame 40, the Daffy done awkwardly.
Frame 41, the back flip let go awkwardly: bolt upright, arms up.
Frame 42, the forward flip let go awkwardly: arched over, the skis askew.
Frame 45, the back scratch done awkwardly.
Frame 44, the mule kick done awkwardly.
Frame 43, the swan done awkwardly.
The bytes frame_table gives as frame 47: not a whole frame, they run on into frame 48 and draw scattered dots. No script shows frame 47.
Frame 48, the third fall: thrown out of the skis, which stick upright in the snow.
Frame 49, the third fall: flying on without the skis.
Frame 50, the third fall: landing on the front in a spray of snow.
Frame 51, the third fall's end: lying flat beside the upright skis.
Frame 52, the fourth fall's start: upright, leaning back.
Frame 53, the fourth fall: skis shooting forward.
Frame 54, the fourth fall: flat on the back in the air.
Frame 55, the fourth fall: landing on the back, skis up.
Frame 56, the fourth fall: sliding on the back.
Frame 57, the fourth fall's end: lying in the snow, skis crossed.
Frame 0, the skier crouched at the top of the in-run, the first frame of every run.
Frame 1, the tuck down the in-run.
Frame 2, rising off the kicker.
Frame 3, the back flip's start: standing, leaning back.
Frame 4, the back flip: arms up, leaning back.
Frame 5, the back flip: arched back.
Frame 6, the back flip: level in the air, head first.
Frame 7, the back flip: upside down.
Frame 8, the back flip: level the other way, coming round.
Frame 9, arms up and skis level: the pose between moves and the only one to land in.
Frame 10, the forward flip's start: diving forward.
Frame 11, the forward flip: tucked, head down.
Frame 12, the forward flip: tucked, upside down.
Frame 13, the forward flip: coming round.
Frame 14, the forward flip's end: level in the air, head down.
Frame 15, standing straight, arms down: the start of every stunt.
Frame 16, the Daffy: legs apart, forward and back.
Frame 17, the Daffy: the legs wide apart.
Frame 17's bytes from $4000 on.
Frame 18, the Daffy held.
Frame 19, coming out of the Daffy: legs apart, arms up.
Frame 20, arms up, leaning: back from the Daffy.
Frame 21, the back scratch's start: knees bending.
Frame 22, the back scratch: skis going back.
Frame 23, the back scratch: skis up behind.
Frame 24, a crouch in the air with the skis pointing down, which no script shows.
Frame 25, coming out of the back scratch.
Frame 26, the back scratch held: the skis touching the back.
The picture's bitmap, packed for unpack_stream: to $A000-$BF3F, the mountains, the hill, the kicker and the crowd. Its first kilobyte fills character rows 0 to 6, the sky and the peaks.
The packed bitmap from row 6 to row 11, the mountains' slopes.
The packed bitmap from row 11 to row 16, the hill, the kicker and the stands.
The packed bitmap from row 16 to row 20, the crowd and the landing slope.
The packed bitmap's last rows, 20 to 24, the snow at the bottom.
The picture's screen colours, packed: to $8000-$83E7.
The picture's colour RAM, packed: to $D800-$DBE7.

The scoreboard's bitmap, four character rows put over the top of the picture for the marks: the eight judges' countries (URS, YUG, FRG, ITA, SUI, GDR, USA, CAN) and TOTAL above an empty row for the marks.
The scoreboard, its second 256 bytes.
The scoreboard, its third 256 bytes.
The scoreboard, its fourth 256 bytes.
The scoreboard, its last 256 bytes.

The sound engine's six slots, 32 bytes each, a sound playing in each: +0 the SID voice it plays on (0 to 2), bit 7 set when the slot is idle; +1-2 the script's address; +3 the frames until its next step; +4 a loop count; +5-6 its return stack's pointer; +8 to +14 its copy of the voice's seven registers (frequency, pulse width, control, attack-decay, sustain-release); +15 a flag that restarts the envelope; +16 its transposition; +17 a fine tuning; +18-21 a frequency slide (step, count, rate); +22-25 a pulse-width sweep (step, period, count). The file holds leftover bytes here, which stop_all clears.
Slot 0's script address (+1 and +2), the base start_sound writes each slot's through.
The script address's high byte.
Slot 0's count of frames to its next step (+3).
Slot 0's transposition, tuning, slide and sweep (+16 to +25), which start_sound clears for the slot it starts.
Slots 2 and 3.
Slots 4 and 5.
The slot count of sound_step's loops.
One byte for each SID voice: set once a slot has written the voice this frame, so a slot numbered higher wins a voice over a lower one.
Voice 1's claim.
Voice 2's claim.
Nonzero while the engine runs; start_sound clears it while it writes a slot.
The filter's registers, copied to $D415-$D418 every frame: the cutoff's low and high bytes, the resonance and the voices filtered, the filter mode and the volume.
The cutoff's high byte, for $D416.
The resonance and the voices filtered, for $D417.
The filter mode and the volume, for $D418.
The six slots' return stacks for the scripts' calls, 16 bytes each.
start_sound's copies of X and Y.
start_sound's copy of Y.
Three bytes nothing reads.
The counters of the two arpeggio routines at $65C2 and $65E4, which nothing calls.
The second arpeggio routine's counter.
The S key's switch: a press sets it to 1 when it is 0, and clears it, stopping every sound, when it is not; nothing else reads it. The file holds $77 here, so the first press stops the sounds.

Starts sound A (100 and above are ignored) from snd_table: its first byte is the slot it plays in, its second the SID voice; the slot's script starts at its third byte on the next step, with the slot's transposition, tuning, slide and sweep cleared. A sound already playing in that slot is cut off.
Steps the slot pointer at $80-$81; nothing calls it.
Steps the script pointer at $82-$83.
Steps the pointer at $86-$87 through a sound's first bytes.
The S key's debounce count, 0 to 2.

The sound engine, once a frame from the interrupt. First the S key, read through CIA 1 (row 1, column 5): pressed after a release, it turns snd_s_key over. The event's start-up makes port A of CIA 1 an input (it writes 0 to $DC02), so the engine's write there drives no row; the key is seen only while joystick 2 is held down, which pulls row 1 low on the same line.
For each of the six slots that is not idle: the frequency slide (snd_slide), the pulse-width sweep, and, when its count of frames runs out, the next step of its script (script_step).
The slide: the rate taken from the count, and the step added to the frequency when it passes zero.

The pulse-width sweep: every frame the step is added to the pulse width, and turned round each time the period runs out. A slip makes it change only the width's low byte: the high byte's add goes to the low byte too, with no INY between.
The slot's frames counted down; at zero its script runs on.

Copies the slots to the SID, from slot 5 down to 0: each voice takes the registers of the highest slot that plays on it, and a slot's restart flag turns the gate off and on again to restart the envelope. Then the filter's four registers.
The SID's three voices' register addresses, $D400, $D407 and $D40E.
The voices' register addresses' high bytes, read one on from sid_voices.
Stops every sound: the slots and their stacks cleared, each slot idle with its stack pointer set, volume 15 with the low-pass mode and nothing filtered, and the SID's voice registers cleared.
The six slots' stack addresses.
Writes 0 to the SID's registers $D400-$D415.
An arpeggio: sets the slot's transposition from the next of 16 steps in snd_arp_table_one. Nothing calls it.
Its 16 transpositions in semitones.
Another, for two slots side by side, from snd_arp_table_two. Nothing calls it either.
Its 16 transpositions.

Runs a slot's script from ($82) until it waits. A byte under $80 is a note: its pitch (set_note), then a byte of how many frames it lasts, and the gate on with the envelope restarted. From $80 a command, its number in the low seven bits, through snd_commands; numbers above 28 stop the sound (cmd_stop).
Steps past a command's last byte and runs the next.
An RTS after snd_continue that nothing reaches.
A note: its pitch, its length, the gate on.
Steps past the length, then sets the restart flag and the gate on.

The 29 commands' routines: 0 set the loop count, 1 loop to an address while the count lasts, 2 start another sound, 3 call machine code, 4 jump to an address, 5 call a part of a script, 6 return from it, 7 end, 8 stop, 9 transpose, 10 tune, 11 jump to machine code, 12 a note with a pulse width, 13 a tied note (no new envelope), 14 the gate off for a time, 15 attack-decay and sustain-release, 16 the waveform and envelope, 17 the pulse width, pulse waveform and envelope, 18 a raw frequency for a time, 19 the slide off, 20 the sweep, 21 the slide, 22 the volume, 23 the resonance, 24 the cutoff, 25 the filter mode, 26 the voices filtered, 27 cutoff, mode and resonance from three bytes, 28 cutoff, resonance and routing, and mode.
The command routines' high bytes, read one on from snd_commands.
Command 11: jumps to the machine code at the next two bytes; its RTS ends the slot's step.
Command 3: calls the machine code at the next two bytes, then goes on with the script.
Jumps through $84-$85.
Back from the machine code to the next command.
Command 7: the slot goes idle.
Command 8, and any number above 28: the slot's registers cleared, the gate left on with no waveform, and two frames later the end command at snd_end_byte.
Command 7 ($87), where cmd_stop points the script.

Sets the slot's frequency from a note byte: the high four bits the octave, the low four the semitone, plus the slot's transposition, from note_freqs shifted right once for each octave under 7; 15 gives the highest frequency, $FFFF, for noise. The slot's fine tuning is added.

The SID frequencies of 24 semitones from C in the top octave: C is $430F, which is 1046.5 Hz on an NTSC machine and two-thirds of a semitone flat on a PAL one, as in the opening ceremony's and the menu's tables.
The frequencies' high bytes, read one on from note_freqs.
Eight bytes of code nothing reaches: a read, a step and a read.
Command 16: the control byte (waveform and gate), attack-decay and sustain-release.
Command 17: the pulse width, then the pulse waveform with the gate ($41), attack-decay and sustain-release.
Command 18: a frequency of two bytes, then a length and the gate on.
A note's length, then the gate on.
Command 4: the script goes on at the next two bytes.
Command 1: the loop count less one; until it reaches 0 the script goes back to the next two bytes' address, then on past them.
Command 0: sets the loop count.
Command 2: starts another sound, often the other voices of a tune.
Command 5: pushes the address after the command onto the slot's stack and goes to the next two bytes' address.
Command 6: back to the address on the slot's stack.
Command 9: the slot's transposition, in semitones.
Command 10: the slot's fine tuning, added to every frequency.
Command 22: the volume, the low four bits of $D418.
Command 24: the filter's cutoff, high byte.
Command 25: the filter mode, the high four bits of $D418.
Command 26: which voices go through the filter, the low four bits of $D417.
Command 23: the resonance, the high four bits of $D417.
Command 27: the cutoff from the first byte and the top bit of the second, the mode from the second's low four bits and the cutoff's low bits from its high four, then the resonance and routing.
Two bytes the filter commands work in.
The filter command's second byte, kept while it works.

Command 21: the slide's rate (255 for every frame) and its step of two bytes, added to the frequency at that rate: the rate is taken from a count each frame, and each time the count passes zero the step is added.
Command 20: the sweep's period and its step.
A note command no table entry reaches: pitch, length, gate.
Command 13: a new pitch and length with no new envelope, the notes tied.
A pulse-width command no table entry reaches.
Command 15: attack-decay and sustain-release.
Command 14: the gate off, and a wait of the next byte's frames.
Command 12: a note with the pulse width's high byte, then its length.
Command 19: the slide stopped.
Command 28: the cutoff's high byte, the resonance and routing, and the mode.
The addresses of the event's 31 sounds, by number, for start_sound. Each sound is a slot, a SID voice and a script. Numbers 1 to 3 and 16 to 22 point to one that does nothing.
The sounds' addresses' high bytes, read one on from snd_table.
Sound 4, the tick as each judge's mark goes up: a short triangle blip sliding down, then a little noise.
Sound 23, a short sliding triangle note on voice 1, which nothing starts.
Sound 14, the fourth fall's: two bursts of noise, the second low and rising, with sound 24 on voice 1.
Sound 13, the third fall's: a burst of noise, then noise sliding down and up, with sound 24.
Sound 24, voice 1 under the third and fourth falls: two short triangle notes, rising then falling.
Sound 11, the first fall's: a burst of noise, then a long low noise rising, with sounds 26 and 27.
Sound 27, voice 2 under the first two falls: four triangle notes, played with bit 7 of $D418 set, which takes voice 3 out of the output unless the filter routes it, then that bit cleared.
Sound 26, voice 1 under the first fall: a triangle note sliding down.
Sound 12, the second fall's: like the first, with sounds 25 and 27.
Sound 25, voice 1 under the second fall: two triangle notes sliding down.
Sound 15, the push off at the start: a burst of noise.
Sound 9, a good landing: a long noise, the skis on the snow.
The sound for the unused numbers: slot 0, voice 2, and an immediate stop.
Sound 10, the crowd's cheer for a mark of 9.0 or more: noise through the high-pass filter for 224 frames, with sound 28.
Sound 28, voice 1 under the cheer: three triangle notes each sliding up and down, like whistles.
Sound 5, the back scratch's and the swan's: a triangle note bending up and back.
Sound 6, an awkward move or a fall: a filtered pulse note bending down.
Sound 7, the Daffy's and the mule kick's: a triangle note, then five falling ones.
Sound 8, a flip's: a pulse note through the band-pass filter, sliding up then down.
The tune's second phrase, for voice 0: after a rest of 256 frames, pulse notes and short rests.
The tune's first phrase: the same rest, then pulse notes, two of them tied by a slide.

Sound 0, the event's tune, at the start and after the marks: voice 0's part, which starts sounds 29 and 30 for the other voices, then plays the two phrases round and round until the sounds are stopped.
Sound 29, the tune's percussion on voice 2: filtered noise, a low note and hits at the top frequency, round and round.
Sound 30, the tune's bass on voice 1: two long pulse notes, round and round.
The file's last 83 bytes, after the sounds, which nothing reads: a fill pattern of $FF, $FE, $01 and $00 like the rest of the slots' leftover bytes.
